STEP 2 · EXPLORE

Solids, liquids, gases and the changes between them

5 – 15 min · Question 1

📺 Watch and learn

Watch before you answer, or afterwards to check your understanding. Plays here, inside the lesson.

Freezing point, melting point and boiling pointPeekaboo Kidz · 6:26 · plays here

🎬 Videos for this lesson

▶ Melting: melting points and freezing points (Oak National Academy)What happens to the particles when ice melts, and why at 0 °C
▶ Boiling and condensing (Oak National Academy)What happens when water boils, and how steam turns back into water
  • SOLID: particles packed tightly in rows. They only vibrate. LIQUID: close together but can slide past each other. GAS: far apart, moving fast in all directions.
  • MELTING: solid → liquid (heat in). Ice melts at 0 °C, its MELTING POINT. FREEZING: liquid → solid (heat out), also at 0 °C.
  • EVAPORATING: liquid → gas at the SURFACE, at any temperature (puddles drying). BOILING: liquid → gas ALL THROUGH the liquid, with bubbles, at the BOILING POINT: 100 °C for water.
  • CONDENSING: gas → liquid (heat out), like drops on a cold window. SUBLIMATION: solid → gas without melting first, like dry ice.

STEP 3 · TEST

The practical: heat ice and record the temperature

15 – 40 min · Question 2
  • 1. Goggles on. Half fill a 250 cm³ beaker with crushed ice.
  • 2. Clamp the thermometer so the bulb is in the middle of the ice, not touching the glass.
  • 3. Read the temperature and write it next to 0 minutes.
  • 4. Switch on the hotplate and start the stopwatch.
  • 5. Every minute: stir gently, read the temperature, and write what you SEE (ice / ice and water / water / bubbles / boiling).
  • 6. Keep going until the water has boiled for 2 minutes (about 14 minutes). Switch OFF the hotplate and leave everything to cool.
  • Jobs: TIMEKEEPER calls "Read!" every minute; READER reads at eye level; RECORDER writes. Swap halfway.

STEP 4 · EXPLAIN

Why does the graph go flat?

40 – 50 min · Question 3
  • Your graph has two FLAT parts: the temperature stops rising even though the hotplate is still on.
  • Flat part 1, about 0 °C: the ice is MELTING. The heat energy pulls the particles out of their rows, so it does not make them hotter.
  • Flat part 2, about 100 °C: the water is BOILING. The heat energy pulls the particles far apart into a gas.
  • Between the flat parts there is only one state (water), so the heat makes the particles move faster and the temperature rises.
  • RULE TO REMEMBER: while a substance is CHANGING STATE, its temperature stays the same.
Show it your way. Write each answer in a sentence, OR label your own graph with the state on each part and an arrow to each flat part, OR explain your graph to a partner and then write one sentence for each part.
